title.narrative: Sustainable Solutions to Solid Waste CXB

description.narrative:
The Project has two components, each with specific key outcomes:
1. Solid Waste Management (SWM) component Developing Waste Management Systems: Vulnerable people from refugee and host communities have enhanced access to appropriate waste management services and infrastructure, and live in cleaner, healthier and more humane conditions.
Changing Behaviours and Attitudes: Local waste management behaviours and practices reformed to be more environmentally and health conscious, to prompt a sustainable change in how waste in the affected regions is created, stored and managed.
2. District Development Planning (DDP) component For the DDP component, which is now expanded as the District Development and Growth Priorities (DDGP) - SDG localisation, the key outcome is an agreed framework and modality for localization of the SDGs and district development needs and growth prioritization in 6 districts of Bangladesh. The results include improved alignment between local needs and plans and national priorities; and strengthened capacity by the GoB, districts, upazilas and partners for monitoring and determining progress of "localisation" of national plans.

UNDP's Country office in Bangladesh has applied to Sida for financing to carry out the intervention "Sustainable Solutions to Solid Waste: A Local Response to the Rohingya crisis in Bangladesh" during the period 2018-2021.
The intervention aims to develop and implement a Solid Waste Management strategy to contribute to improved environment, health, water quality, sanitation, recycling, livelihoods and human dignity in areas of Cox's bazar District affected by the Rohingya refugee crisis.
The project has two outcomes:
1. Developing Waste Management Systems: Vulnerable people from refugee and host communities have enhanced access to appropriate waste management services and infrastructure, and live in cleaner, healthier and more humane conditions.
2. Changing Behaviours and Attitudes: Local waste management behaviours and practices reformed to be more environmentally and health conscious, to prompt a sustainable change in how waste in the affected regions is created, stored and managed.
UNDP together with its implementing partners (NGOs and Local Government agencies) will implement the intervention. UNDP’s proposed project will tie innovative solid waste activities to well-defined environmental, health, WASH, site management, and protection goals (both under the Joint Response Plan and the SDGs), with significant additional anticipated benefits to livelihoods, social cohesion, gender, and human dignity in Cox’s Bazar District.
This will be done through a deliberately phased approach, to respond effectively to pressing and urgent waste removal needs in the short-term. In parallel the project will engage refugees and people in host communities as well as government to design and develop longer-term recycling activities to expand and nurture a local economy for solid waste and generate livelihood benefits and income for local people. This is in line with the vision outlined in the Rohingya Joint Response Plan, which states that at the present “stage of the response, solid waste management programs will be supported by Cash-Based Interventions for waste collection, [while in time] a solid waste management system will be established including the installation, operation and maintenance of a shared landfill”. Households, including women, will be prominently engaged as the most critical local unit, as it is at the household and family level that much of the current waste is produced, and it is at this level that solutions must be applied.
The construction of new infrastructure and support to recycling enterprises is expected to transform the existing solid waste management options on the ground. When the profitable incentives for household recycling and waste disposal are adjusted, permanent changes in local behavior, waste disposal, recycling patterns, and effective waste management systems will result. This will improve the local environment and health for all people in affected communities, removing potential sources of toxins and danger to both the water supply, the physical landscape, and the air (by preventing the burning of trash), while providing added benefits to the local economy.
UNDP and partners are envisioned to show how waste can be turned into benefits and livelihoods development. Recycling and repurposing of solid waste can be a lucrative industry with transformative potential for vulnerable people and communities. These sorts of “trash-to-cash” activities will encourage local people in both host communities and refugee camps to view solid waste as a potential resource. Improvements to the management of waste, and a cleaner local landscape, are visible and demonstrable improvements in conditions for local communities, and can contribute to reinforce social cohesion.
The intervention’s total budget is 4 879 764 USD, approximately 45 million SEK. Sida will provide 100% of the total project budget.

UNDP:s landskontor i Bangladesh har ansökt om finansiering för att utföra insatsen "Hållbara lösningar för avfallshantering: en lokal respons på Rohingya-krisen i Bangladesh" under perioden 2018–2021.
Insatsen syftar till att utveckla och genomföra ett hållbart avfallshanteringssystem för att bidra till förbättrad miljö, hälsa, vattenkvalitet, sanitet, återvinning, försörjning, social sammanhållning och mänsklig värdighet inom områden av Cox Bazar som påverkas av flyktingkrisen.
Projektet har två övergripande resultat:
1. Utveckla ett hållbart avfallshanteringssystem: Utsatta människor från flykting- och värdsamhällen har förbättrad tillgång till lämplig avfallshantering och infrastruktur, och lever i renare, friskare och mer humana förhållanden.
2. Förändra beteenden och attityder: Lokala avfallshanteringsmetoder och beteenden förändras till det bättre och blir mer miljö-och hälsomedvetna, för att skapa en hållbar förändring i hur avfall i området uppkommer, lagras och hanteras.
UNDP kommer tillsammans med sina partners (icke-statliga organisationer och lokala myndigheter) att genomföra insatsen. Projektet kommer att knyta innovativa avfallshanteringsmetoder till mål inom miljö, hälsa, vatten och sanitet, lägerplanering och skydd (enligt den gemensamma handlingsplanen för Rohingya-krisen och de globala utvecklingsmålen), med betydande resultat för försörjningsmöjligheter, social sammanhållning, jämlikhet, och mänsklig värdighet i Cox Bazar.
Detta kommer att ske genom en stegvis implementering för att effektivt möta angelägna och brådskande behov av avfallshantering på kort sikt. Parallellt kommer projektet att engagera flyktingar och människor i värdsamhällen samt statliga myndigheter för att utforma och utveckla långsiktiga återvinningsaktiviteter för att expandera den lokala ekonomin inom avfall och generera försörjningsmöjligheter och inkomster för lokalbefolkningen. Detta i enlighet med visionen i den gemensamma handlingsplanen för Rohingya-krisen, som säger att ”i det nuvarande stadiet kommer avfallshantering stödjas av kontantbaserade aktiviteter för insamling av avfall, [medan längre fram] kommer ett avfallshanteringssystem att etableras vilket inkluderar installation, drift och underhåll av en gemensam deponi". Hushåll, och särskilt kvinnor, kommer att engageras, eftersom det är på hushålls-och familjenivå som det mesta av avfallet produceras, och det är där som lösningar måste tillämpas.
Konstruktion av ny infrastruktur och stöd till återvinningsföretag förväntas omvandla befintliga avfallshanteringsalternativ på lokal nivå. När lönsamma incitament för hushållsåtervinning och avfallshantering införs kommer det leda till förändringar i beteende, avfallshantering och återvinningsmönster. Detta kommer att förbättra lokal miljö och hälsa för alla människor i drabbade samhällen, reducera potentiella föroreningskällor och faror för både vattenförsörjning, det fysiska landskapet och luften (genom att minska förbränning av sopor) samtidigt som det ger extra fördelar för lokal ekonomi.
UNDP och partners kommer med denna insats att visa hur avfall kan omvandlas till positiva fördelar och försörjningsmöjligheter. Återvinning och återanvändning av avfall kan vara en lukrativ industri med transformativ potential för utsatta människor och samhällen. Detta kommer att uppmuntra människor i både värdsamhällen och flyktingläger att se avfall som en potentiell resurs. Förbättringar av avfallshantering och en renare miljö är synliga och påtagliga förbättringar av förhållandena för lokalsamhällen och kan bidra till att stärka den sociala sammanhållningen.
Insatsens totala budget är 4 879 764 USD (cirka 45 miljoner kronor). Sida finansierar 100% av den totala projektbudgeten.

title.narrative: Sustainable Solutions to Solid Waste Cox's Bazar

description.narrative:
Highlights of results/progress reported by UNDP.
Outcome: Developing Waste Management Systems.
Benefits to refugee camps
The Sanitary Landfill in Ukhia camps has contributed to provide a safe place where waste from camps can be finally disposed of after recovering the organic and recyclable material. Before the construction of this facility, camps had no other option than to deal with the waste being generated. Due to the lack of space in camps, many WASH NGOs were forced to practise open incineration, open dumping, and burying waste. Gradually camps are using the landfill and changing these practices (85% of the total camps). As the landfill is only used for inorganic waste, camps are requested to conduct proper segregation of organic and recyclables which contribute to the production of compost and supports the local recycling sector.
A survey of perceptions was conducted among the WASH partners to know the level of satisfaction with the facility. Among the survey respondents using the landfill, 90% expressed satisfaction over the existence and utilisation of the facility.
To maximize the use of the landfill, the project, in coordination with the WASH sector, will continue advocating for the use of the landfill and supporting the camps with the project trucks when required.
The sanitary landfill has supported three main critical activities over the last year: 1) cleaning campaign of 26 camps, 2) regular waste disposal for 23 camps and 3) absorbing the emergency waste from 3 fire events affecting 5 camps in 2021 and 2022. In total, about 12,461 m3 of waste has been safely disposed in the sanitary landfill and avoided additional environmental impacts and health hazards.
Benefits to host communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf
The established SWM systems in the Unions Parishads and Teknaf Municipality have resulted in the collection and safe disposal of 47,775m3 of waste up to February 2022 (which accounts for more than 100% of the project target: 34,000 m3). This represents 82% of the total waste generated from 5,236 HH and 5,390 market shops. In total, 23% of the collected waste has been recovered before landfilling: 6,025 m3 organic converted into compost and 126 m3 recyclables transferred to the recycling dealers. Before the project, all beneficiarys waste was literally dumped into open spaces or rivers as they did not have any other alternative system.
In terms of beneficiarys perceptions, 92% of the direct beneficiaries are satisfied with the waste collection service in place; 82.3% feel that the overall livelihoods could be improved by a clean and healthy environment. Regarding the continuity of the service, 83% of them said they would pay for such a waste management system and allow the daily collection of waste from their place (HH: 82.5% and shop: 83.9%).
Outcome: Changing behaviors and attitudes
Benefits to refugee camps
At the camp level, at least 85% of the Ukhia camps have consolidated their SWM systems and do segregate their waste and recover organic and recyclables at camp level. At the response level, UNDP has contributed to set strategies and practises, built awareness and understanding among partners, and put the SWM on the Inter-Sector Consultative Group (ISCG) agenda as a cross-sector related-topic. One success is the work implemented by the Inter-sector SWM Group which is giving support to the sector coordinators in identifying best practises for waste reduction and proper management among their sector partners
Benefits to host communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf
The direct project beneficiaries formed by HH and shops have gained a clear understanding on the classification of the waste they generated (88% of respondents) and where they must put their waste (97%). However, it seems that the knowledge is not yet put into practise in most of the cases, as only 67.3% (HH: 70.4%, shops: 64.5%) segregate waste regularly. When it comes to the organic waste, 97.2% of the HH respondents dispose organic waste in green bins, whereas the percentage is lower for shops, only 59.4%. Regarding the inorganic waste, 42% of the HHs were disposing of inorganic waste in blue bins, and only 14.3% of the shop had this practice. HH and shops are still mixing the inorganic waste with organic. However, the positive result is that only 8,7% of beneficiaries dispose of waste other than bins or community bins and litter it in open spaces.
After the communication campaign, and based on the end-line survey, the beneficiaries have gained a better understanding of the concept of 3Rs (Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle), as 62% of the respondents had knowledge of it in comparison to only 36.3% in August 2021.
Outcome: Improved alignment between local needs and plans and national priorities
The project is succeeding to prepare the first ever district-level development plan in Bangladesh using the bottom-up inclusive approach (including youth, women, ethnic minorities, fisherfolk, etc.) The district development plan is organised around short (one year) and medium term (five years) priorities, and targets were also framed around indicators of the SDGs. All eight Upazilas, 71 Unions (639 Wards), 4 Municipalities of CXB have been engaged, and there is strong buy-in from local stakeholders, including the District Commissioner's Office. One of the main hurdles is data availability as the basis for DDPs. The project managed to collect data from all unions and municipalities, including developing a geographic information mapping (GIS) system for the whole CXB district. As a result of the planning, identified priorities of CXB district amounting to 4.61 MUSD were included in the UN Joint Response Plan 2021, a 3-fold increase from the previous year's JRP. UNDP has proposed to replicate the experience and learnings of the DDP process in CXB to other districts with high levels of vulnerabilities, namely, Patuakhali, Feni, Natore and Kurigram.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
